Groups (e.g., product types, months, or cities) are usually represented on the x axis.
Measurements (e.g., sales numbers, temperatures, or percentages) are usually represented on the y axis.

Rank items from largest to smallest
, for example a company’s top ten customers by spend, most common causes of support tickets, bestselling book titles, or the leading sources of a country’s emissions.
Compare a measurement variable over two or more grouping variables
, for example quarterly revenue split by product line, survey answers by response option, budget by spending category across several years, or population by age band in each country.
Show deviation above and below a baseline with diverging bars
, for example actual vs. budgeted spend per team, temperature anomalies by year, net sentiment scores by topic, or percentage change in sales by store.
Compare values across a small number of discrete time periods
, for example annual profit for the last five years, quarterly enrollment, or headcount at the end of each fiscal year. In this case, time periods act as grouping variables.

children.value: Because the group data are unique, we can create a rudimentary bar chart just by converting the measurement value into a string.
To do this, we can use the handy
method, which iterates over each row, returning the row index and row values each time.

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '|')
We can improve the display by using the block character █ instead of a pipe:

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '█')
We can even add the number value to make it more legible.

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '█' + " " + str(row['measure']))
And — voilà! — you have a bar chart.

plt.show()

Let’s clean the figure up a bit.
First, let’s remove the legend since it is not really needed in this example.
Second, let’s rotate the letters on the x axis for readability.

df1.plot(kind='bar', x='group', y='measure', 
         title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", 
         legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()

, Pandas will use the index as the x axis.

df1.plot.bar(y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)

In fact, it is a good practice to assign the grouping variable to be the index in this case.
Since the values are unique, they can used as index values.

df2 = df1.set_index('group')
df2.plot.bar(y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)

In the preceding example we had a data set in which unique grouping values are paired with measurements.
In reality, we don’t often get data like this. More typically, the grouping values are repeated over observations.
